items.text: SEASON 6 · EPISODE 6 · DRAFT  Design studio and the Playhouse · Maya, Anselm and Odile · Level L4 · Intermediate support  The Playhouse is beautiful — and every line of dialogue lasts two seconds. The architect loves the plaster. The finishes freeze Friday.  ⚑ RV-141: figures illustrative. Finishes are the architect’s; fire ratings the fire engineer’s. Some choices run on a clock.

items.title: Hard Walls
items.stakes: The Playhouse is beautiful and every line of dialogue lasts two seconds. The architect loves the plaster; the finishes freeze Friday.
items.reward: Words that carry, plaster that stays, and an architect who says yes.

objectives.text: Work out why the plaster stays
Make acoustics part of the finishes
Look closer: two things about the Playhouse

items.rumor: The fix had been sitting in the interior package the whole time, pretending to be decoration.

items.alt: The Playhouse at the first reading in the house: the artistic director at the lip of the stage, Anselm in the stalls with a sound-level meter.

bubbles.text: I can hear every word twice. The second time is worse.

items.text: ✦ UX RULE #57 · AVERY'S LENS  Work with the room's intent  The best fix serves everyone's goal — the architect's look, the director's words and the audience's ears — not one of them at the others' cost.  Covering Odile's plaster would have fixed the reverb and wrecked the room. Her own ‘decorative panels’ fixed it and kept the room.

items.alt: Odile, the architect, arms wide at the bare lime-plaster walls; Maya beside her with a clipboard.

bubbles.text: It is. It's also most of the problem.

items.prompt: Before you say it: the plaster stays. It's a listing condition and I spent two years on it.

options.label: “It should — near the stage it helps the actors. Can we talk about the rear walls and your decorative panels?”
options.reply: …You read my interior package. Go on.

options.label: “The room doesn't work. Something has to give.”
options.reply: Then find something that isn't my plaster.

options.label: “What's the plaster doing for you?”
options.reply: Light, texture, history. What's it doing for you?

items.prompt: Tuesday morning. The room is too live for speech. How do you start?
items.risk: A playhouse where nobody can follow a play.
timeout: Wednesday arrives with no target and no numbers.
Friday freezes the plaster as it is.

hints.text: Whose goal is it, and how far are we from it?

options.label: Specify a bigger sound system so the words are louder
options.fail: You can't amplify your way out of reverberation.

options.label: Measure, agree a target with the director and the acoustician, and calculate the absorption needed
options.result: ≈ 1.8 s occupied; target 0.85–1.05 s; about 370 m² more absorption.
options.consequence: Goal, room, numbers — in that order.

options.label: Cover the plaster in foam
options.result: Odile: “That plaster is a listing condition and my design. No.”
options.consequence: Someone else's design and someone else's consent.

options.label: Tell the director the actors should project more

items.title: Not the plaster.
items.body: The listing officer's condition 7 keeps the historic plaster on the proscenium and side walls — and near the stage it's useful: early reflections help the actors be heard. The late reflections that blur the words come off the rear wall and the upper side walls — new work, free to treat.
items.label: Test: why does the plaster stay — and where does absorption help?

items.sub: Intermediate · the skill behind this chapter

items.alt: A teaching moment: Anselm and Odile beside a board. Sabine: point one six one times the volume, over the absorption. Volume in cubic metres, absorption in square metres. Four thousand cubic metres, three hundred and fifty of absorption… about one point eight seconds. For a play? Too long for speech. About three hundred and fifty more gets us near point nine — and I promise it can be beautiful.

items.title: Sabine's cushions
items.body: In 1895 Harvard asked a young physics instructor, Wallace Sabine, to fix a lecture hall nobody could understand. He carried seat cushions from a nearby theatre in and out at night, timing how long an organ pipe's note lingered. His measurements became RT60 = 0.161 V ÷ A — the formula on this page.

items.alt: A long section of the Playhouse: the stage and its plaster at left, the rear wall and upper side walls at right marked ‘decorative panels over MDF’. RT60 ≈ 1.8 s occupied.
items.caption: Three hundred square metres of fabric — over MDF.

items.title: Condition 7
items.body: The listing officer's consent letter, condition 7: *historic lime plaster to the proscenium and side walls to be retained and exposed.* The rear wall and the upper side walls are new work — and free.

items.title: Already paid for.
items.body: Odile's own interior package: 300 m² of ‘decorative fabric panels’ on the rear and upper side walls — fabric stretched over 18 mm MDF, which reflects almost everything. Put 50 mm of mineral wool and an air gap behind the same fabric, and they become about 250 m² of extra absorption; the heavy rear curtain Odile already specified makes up the rest.
items.label: Test: how much do the panels add — and what changes on them?

items.prompt: Wednesday. Where does the absorption go?
items.happening: 300 m² of panels in the package.
items.risk: A fix that spoils the room or fails the fire rating.
timeout: Friday's freeze passes with MDF behind the fabric.

hints.text: Which surfaces, which build-up, and whose approval?

options.label: Re-specify Odile's panels as fire-rated absorbers on the rear and upper side walls, keep the plaster near the stage, and ask the fire engineer to confirm the rating
options.result: Odile: “Same fabric, same pattern? Then yes.” The fire engineer confirms.
options.consequence: Her design, a new job, everybody's goal.

options.label: Panels on every wall, including around the stage
options.result: The actors sound dry and small; the back rows lose them.
options.consequence: Too much, in the wrong place.

options.label: Add more panels but leave the MDF behind the fabric
options.result: Decoration with extra steps — nothing changes.
options.consequence: What's behind the fabric is the absorber.

options.label: Let the contractor pick an absorber at submittal
options.result: The contractor picks the cheapest foam. It fails the fire rating.
options.consequence: The design decision left the design.
options.fail: Fire ratings aren't a submittal afterthought.

items.label: **Put it in order:** treat a room without spoiling it.

items.alt: The same section after the change: the rear wall and upper side walls in indigo as absorbers, the plaster near the stage kept. RT60 ≈ 0.95 s occupied.
items.caption: Same fabric. Different room.

items.prompt: Friday. How does acoustics stop being a surprise on the next project?
known: ◉ Absorption was hiding in the finishes
items.risk: Another beautiful room nobody can hear in.
timeout: The next room starts at 1.8 s too.

options.label: An acoustic target in the brief, absorption called out in the architect's finishes schedule, and a measurement at handover
options.result: Odile adds an ‘acoustic’ column to her finishes schedule template.
options.consequence: Intent written where finishes are decided.

options.label: Anselm reviews every finishes package by eye
Always specify foam everywhere
options.result: Every room sounds dead — and fails the fire engineer.

options.label: Nothing — the Playhouse is fixed
options.result: The courthouse's jury room has the same hard walls.

items.sub: Three months later · the dress rehearsal

items.alt: The dress rehearsal: the director at the lip of the stage, delighted; Odile in the stalls, looking at her plaster and her panels.

items.title: Fabric over MDF
items.body: The interior package's sample panel: a patterned fabric stretched over 18 mm MDF. At speech frequencies MDF reflects almost everything. Swap the MDF for 50 mm of mineral wool and an air gap, and the same fabric becomes one of the best absorbers in the building.

items.alt: The courthouse's Courtroom 1: a high 4.2 m ceiling. Anselm points up at a reflected ceiling plan.

bubbles.text: These loudspeakers are spaced for a three-metre ceiling. This one's four point two.

items.text: FIELD NOTE —  RT60 = 0.161 × V ÷ A. Agree the target, measure, calculate, put absorption where it helps (rear and upper walls) and keep reflective surfaces where they help (near the stage). Look for absorption already in the design — and let the architect and the fire engineer decide what’s theirs. Measure again at the end.
REFLECTION (optional)  · The fix was already in Odile’s package. What have you solved lately by reading someone else’s work more carefully?
